raw_comment:
I notice first in these graphs that each color represents something different, whether it be a record, a current finding, or a prediction. It is obvious that southern states have drastically higher temperatures than northern cities this time of year. In a lot of these cities, people are experiencing drastic temperature fluctuations.  Atlanta, Boston, Minneapolis, and New York are all cities that experienced 30-degree differences in just five days. In other cities, temperatures are not near the expected temperatures, but rather near the record highs and lows. Cities like Dallas, Fort Myers, Orlando, and Tampa all reached temperatures above the normal high. More rare were cities dipping below their normal lows, but it did happen briefly in Denver and Minneapolis.
What I am most curious about in this graph is the cause for such drastic fluctuations in weather and why many cities are experiencing extreme highs and lows in temperature. This is likely in part due to global warming. I am also curious if the cities whose forecasts were rather drastic reached their predicted temperatures. 
This relates to me and my community because we have been experiencing drastic weather ourselves. Here, the weather was nearing zero degrees last week, but just days later it neared 50 degrees. 
A catchphrase for this graph is "Wacky Weather Sweeps the Nation".

I notice that the graph shows the high and low temperatures Dec. 6-10 and the forecasted high and low temperatures for Dec. 11-15. The light gray bars of the graph show the average temperature in past years during this time. Particularly cities on the east coast saw higher than the average temperatures. Cities in the northeast, like Boston that are generally colder, recorded temperatures over 40 degrees for Dec. 6-10. While cities on the west coast experienced lower than the average temperature recorded. 

I wonder if the predicted forecasts were accurate and if they followed similar trends to Dec. 6-10. I also wonder the connections to climate change and global warming. 

This affects my community because I live in New Jersey, which is on the East Coast. New Jersey generally has colder winters, but the weather has been generally warmer, in the 50s and 60s. The lack of snow this season makes me concerned about the affects of global warming on my community.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph shows that each area experienced at least mild fluctuation of the high and low forecasts. Additionally, forecasts for each individual city always correspond at least slightly with the actual temperatures for the previous week. For example, in Denver, the ranges for actual highs and lows experienced a dip Thursday, and the same pattern is seen in the forecast for the next Thursday. Only a few cities greatly stray from this pattern, including Minneapolis, New York, and Portland, Oregon. 

I wonder if weather forecasts are often based on the previous week(s), and exactly what other factors are taken into account. I also wonder how accurate these forecasts ultimately were and if the accuracy of the results affects how forecasts are made in the future.

This relates to me and my community because we are constantly checking weather forecasts in order to decide what to wear, where to go, and what to bring with us.

Headline: Forecasts - How Accurate Are They Really?

raw_comment:
I notice in this graph that the temperatures of some of the areas in the north that would usually experience cold weather at this time, have higher temperatures than normal. Boston had temperatures over 40 degrees for four consecutive days. Additionally, Denver had temperatures reaching 60 degrees and some days forecasted to go over 60. Where areas in the north the temperature is increasing, it is the opposite for places in the south. Both Houston and Phoenix in the southern states of Texas and Arizona dropped to low temperatures reaching 40 and under, which is unlike usual weather during this time. I also notice that while in some areas, the temperatures remain consistent over the days from December 6 to December 10, some areas have varying  drops in temperature. In Boston, it goes from reaching the 50s, to dropping down to almost 20 degrees in the forecast. 
I wonder why some places have greater temperatures drops and rises than others that are more consistent. 
This relates to me and my community because it is noticeable the unnatural temperatures that New Jersey is experiencing in the months of winter that should be colder. The weather has been reaching near the 60s, which is irregular around this time. Last year it was snowing around the same time that the temperatures are rising now. This demonstrates how much global warming is effecting the world. 
Catchy Headline "Highs and Lows: How Global Warming is Affecting the Globe"

raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the high and low temperatures in various cities from December 6-10 and the forecasted temperatures for December 11-15.  The temperatures fluctuated quite a bit and there are some consistencies depending on the area.  For example, New York and Boston are in a relatively similar area and their temperatures increased and decreased in a similar way.  The main thing I notice is how the normal temperatures were quite different than the ones recorded.  Some cities like Detroit and Dallas experienced much higher temperatures than normal.  On the other hand, cities like Los Angeles and Seattle are experiencing lower temperatures.  I wonder what the cause for these changes is.  It is understood that the weather will not be the same every year, but many of these changes are rather drastic.  This affects my community because for certain things to function like the farming system, temperatures must fall under the proper conditions.  If the temperatures begin to negatively affect daily life, there will be detrimental outcomes.  I would entitle this graph: "Abnormal Temperatures."

raw_comment:
These graphs display the highs and lows in temperature between December 6-10, represented by the black bars, and the forecasts for December 11-15, represented by the thin dark gray bars, across 22 locations. The medium gray bars represent normal highs and lows for reach location in years past and the light gray bars represent the record highs and lows. I noticed that in a majority of locations depicted the temperatures were slightly higher than their average. 

I wonder if the predicted forecasts were accurate, or if the real temperatures were actually higher than they predicted.

I observed that some locations temperatures fluctuated more than others. For instance, the daily temperatures of Atlanta between lows of 40 and record breaking lows 60, when their previous average temperatures had a standard low of 40. A majority of the locations were also above their average temperatures. For instance Tampa, Ft. Myers, and Houston all neared their record temperatures.

In my own community I have noticed temperatures that have been higher than average for the beginning of winter. Thus, this graph shows that the changing of temperature has been a national trend.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
With the exception of Florida, which is generally warm year-round, I noticed that states in the east saw a brief period of warmer weather. However, winter-like conditions are once again expected.

What do you wonder?
I'm curious as to why there was a brief increase in warm weather in the eastern states given that there was nothing unusual reported in the news.

How does this relate to you and your community?
Since we live on the east coast and were impacted by that brief warm spell, this is relevant to me and my neighborhood.

What’s going on in this graph?
The Weather from Last Week: The Highs and Lows

|---|---|---|

| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that there are several graphs for many cities on this huge panel. Additionally, some of the graphs show patterns with roughly the same temperature. Especially those that are cities in the same general vicinity. Also, the temperature varies more throughout the day in Florida and California than it does in any other state, even though they should be hot.
What do you wonder?
I wonder as to why they only chose these particular states to test the temperatures. Also, what is the cause of the rise in record temperatures seen in most of the charts, and is it possible that climate change and gloabl warming are contributing to these trends?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because I find it quite intriguing to observe the drastically diverse temperature ranges over a 10-day period, especially in comparison.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that every graph follows a sort of "wave like" pattern. No graphs make a significant drop or increase in temperature. This is most likely because the days are so close to each other which means there is not enough time for such a sudden change. The only one City that does not follow this pattern is Detroit, where on a sunday they had a surge in temperature. More specifically in the city I am closest to (New York) there are a couple days in which the temperature hardly changes. For example the first thursday and saturday. 

2. I wonder why no states in the country go below 0 degrees. Some of these states are understandable because they are normally warm, like Miami, Orlando, and Tampa; but the majority of states are usually around 10-30 degrees this time of year. Is this the effect of global warming?

3. Well if these above average temperatures are the result of global warming there should be some kind of work done to try and fix it. Generally temperature is something that every person should be aware of because of the importance of it in everyday life.

4. "A White or Warm Winter? The Above Average Temperatures of U.S. Cities"

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
1) I noticed that temperatures in the east coast are more prone to variations while those on the western side stay relatively within the norm.  For example, on the first Wednesday in NY, the temperatures reached a high of nearly 60 degrees, and the low was nearly 55 degrees; all while the average highs and lows for that day are between what looks like 38 degrees and 48 degrees. I also noticed that the highest record highs are usually found in the west -- most of the highs in the east coast don't even reach the 80s -- but the lowest record for the lowest temp. is found in Minneapolis, a city in a midwestern state. The longest record range belongs to Denver as well.
2) I wonder if the variations of temperature in the eastern coast are due to some of the states being near more bodies of water compared to the more western states. The temperatures could also depend on whether the state is closer to the equator or the North Pole. I also wondered how global warming has affected the average temperatures compared to those in the past.
3) This relates to me in my community, because although there isn't a city from my state present within the charts, NY is relatively close enough for us to have similar temperatures. Because of that, we've also experienced odd temperatures such as being extremely cold one day and regular temperatures the next. So much so, many of the residents and peers in my town have talked about it.
4) "Weather Predictability; Is There A Notable Difference?"

1. What do you notice?
I notice that in New York, the temperature is around the same throughout all the days shown in the graph with only a few outliers. The highest temperature was about 60 degrees and the lowest forecasted is about 30 degrees. 

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why in New York there can be such a drastic difference in temperature in only a few days. The temperature dropped from 60 degrees to 30 degrees in only about 5 days. I wonder is global warming has anything to do with the random elevations in temperature on the East Coast.

3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because my town is very close to New York. My community and I experience the same temperatures that New York does and we feel the fluctuation in temperatures as well.  The weather causes a change in plans and even the clothes we wear depending on the temperature for the day. 

4. What’s going on in this graph? 
Baby it's Cold Outside; Do You Have to Bundle up This December?

What do you notice?
I noticed that within these graphs of temperatures recorded from these different locations there is a continuous pattern of increasing and decreasing whether it may be slightly or shown by a lot. However it is shown that the cities around the same area will be close to having the same temperature, but is never exactly the same. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder if global warming or climate change could be a possible factor as to why the temperature from these different locations are so up and down.

How does this relate to your community?

What's going on in this graph?

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

|---|---|---|

In the New York temperature graph,  I notice that on most days the temperature is 40 degrees. On the second day, the temperature is the highest at 60 degrees. On the 8th day, it reaches a low temperature of around 30 degrees. I also notice that cities such as Orlando, Miami, and San Diego have higher temperatures compared to New York. Houston seems to have the highest temperature of slightly above 80 degrees. 

 I wonder why some cities have a high temperature one day and the next it's lower by almost degrees. 

This data relates to me and my community because in Perth Amboy the temperature is starting to drop. And it's similar to the weather in New York. 

Weather Through The Country

- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.

- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment:
What do you notice? I notice that in New York, the temperature is pretty much close in range. The highest temperature is in the high 50s almost 60 degrees and the lowest is in the 30s. Although, throughout the week it seems to be colder than the weekend. I would say at least half of the cities have a larger range like New York such as Detroit, Boston, Denver, etc. I would say they show a significant change in temperature throughout the 10 days. 

What do you wonder? I wonder if global warming is a factor in the drastic temperature changes. One day the temperature is high and the next is relatively low. Global warming is known for causing irregularities in temperatures. 

How does this relate to you and your community? This relates to me and my community because New York is our neighbor state. Typically, any temperatures in New York are also felt and affect New Jersey. It is very unusual to experience warm weather in December, yet some days it is freezing. This affects me personally because I am constantly walking to my destinations; everyday I find out if I need my coat or not. 

Headline: Temperature Trends; Warm Winters Incoming

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

Meyers, Orlando, and Miami) as well as the west coast including Seattle, San Fransisco, and San Diego, have much more stable temperatures. I also notice that almost every city has a higher temperature than normal.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

-This is relevant to my neighborhood since New York is close to mines. Any changes in the weather in this city will almost certainly have an impact on my community. Weather has an impact on people's lives all around the world.

-Temperature and reality: is there a relationship?

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the shape of the temperature trends for some graphs have a similiar pattern.  Atlanta, Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Washington, and Seattle all have graphs that increase, decrease, and then increase again. I also notice that the degrees on the side of each graph are different from each other because some cities reached below or above the 40s than others.

2. I wonder what other factors are affecting New York, other than global warming, to affect their temperature. I also wonder how it is possible for some cities could be near each other but still have clearly different temperatures. 

3. This relates to me and my community because New York is somewhat close to where I am. The times I have gone to New York City in december has always been cold, below 30 degrees farenheit. But now, seeing that temperatures have barely even reached 30 degrees farenheit, it is weird to see the big change. 

4. Freezing in December? Not Anymore!

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

1.  - I notice that the graphs go by cities and not states. I also notice that San Francisco, Orlando, Houston, and Tampa seem to have the most consistent temperature trends. While Atlanta, Boston, Denver, and Dallas seem to have the least consistent temperature trends.

	- The Ups and Downs of Weather.

- No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
1. I noted that the graph includes 22 cities and that the chronology runs from December 6 to 15. I also noted that they indicated in the graph background information that they updated the graph on December 12. The cities covered tended to be prominent places in the United States, such as New York City, Chicago, and Atlanta. In addition to reaching some record high temperatures. Cities that lie in the same state also tend to have similar temperature patterns which include the cities of Florida: Miami, Tampa, and Orland. The graphs are based on preliminary data and have a key indicating which shows the lowest temperature and the highest. 
2. I'm curious as to why temperature varies so drastically; could this be linked to global warming or other environmental factors?
3. This is significant to my community and myself since it has the potential to change every day routines and raise new concerns. The fluctuating and unpredictable temperature indicates the impact that humans have on the world as a result of factors such as climate change. This current problem has been produced primarily by humans polluting without being aware of the negative consequences. Climate change has the potential to influence the severity or frequency of current health issues. Furthermore, it may bring new or unanticipated health difficulties in people or places they have never been before. 
4. Unpredictable Weather Change: Will the World Let it Snow This Upcoming Christmas?

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
Francois AP Lang Post

What do we notice? 
The northern states have more of a swing in temperatures than southern states, Denver has a pretty large swing in temperatures compared to Ft. Meyers.

What do we wonder? 
What causes such great fluctuation, why are they studying this, and why is this information important? Does this have something to do with climate change?

How does this affect our community? 
If this is related to global warming, it could be a problem for Wisconsin since we are more of a northern state.

Catchy Titles
Maybe it's (not so) cold outside

- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.

- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.   We did not read any headlines yet that related to the ideas of the graphs.  In fact, the New York Times’ headline “10-Day Temperature Trends” was not very “catchy.”  Also, there is no article accompanying the graphs.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Jan. 13 to see the Reveal with background on the AccuWeather forecasts, some questions about the graphs and a few Stat Nuggets.

We will be off until Friday, Jan. 6, when we will release the next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” for moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 11.  Have a good holiday season.  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 

graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 

Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, where is it about 5 degrees F. colder than forecasted in the graph, and Leigh Nataro of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania where it looks like it is too warm for snow tomorrow.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

1. What do you notice?

	I noticed that the temperature trend graphs vary significantly depending on location. I also noticed that many of the cities that lie in the same state have similar temperature trends such as Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. I also noticed that many of the graphs have reached temperatures of record highs.

2. What do you wonder?

	I wonder what has caused the increased trend in record highs throughout the majority of the graphs and I wonder if climate change and global warming may play a role in these trends. While it’s not exactly surprising, being a resident of Massachusetts, I wonder why the trends for Boston significantly fluctuate from high temperatures to low temperatures throughout the week.

	As a resident of one of these cities, Boston specifically, this impacts day to day activities that we may intend to do be it indoors or outdoors.

	This graph is depicting the various temperature trends across major cities throughout the United States. My catchy headline would be “A Winter Wonderland No More: Multiple Record Highs in Current U.S. Temperature Trends”

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
1. The west coast is around its average temperature but mid America and the east coast are around the higher end. Cities near the coast don’t have huge jumps but cities away from the oceans do much higher highs and lower lows, I believe because of the waters high specific heat temperature. 

2. I wonder why the west coast is around its average temperature and other cities are near its high. 

3. It affects me because the average temperature on the east coast (where I live) is rising, which I would assume means shorter winters and possibly longer tourist season. 

4. Do you need a sweater for the changing weather?

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

|---|---|---|

| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment: I notice that cities in the North that are known for their cooler temperature have had an increase in temperature such as Philidelphia and New York City. I wonder if the change in climate has to do with global warming and the pollution these cities contribute to. This relates to me and my community as I live in New York right outside the city and as I get older, I have noticed the changes in climate. image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the cities that are located in the southern parts of the United States tend to have the highest measured high and low temperatures in comparison to the cities located in northern states which are observed to show colder high temperatures and even colder low temperatures. I also notice that as the month proceeds, the cities typically are and/or will be experiencing a temperature decrease, minus a couple of the cities.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why cities like Boston are experiencing relatively high-temperature trends when the city is located in an area where the average temperature is colder than the range seen in the graph. I wonder if this has to do with climate change and its impact on the cities known to have cooler temperatures than we see in these graphs.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because as the month proceeds, my city will probably experience a temperature decrease which is not good because usually when the temperature drops in the Boston area, there is a higher chance for snowfall.

What is going on in this graph?
These graphs are showcasing the measured high and low temperatures of certain cities and the predicted high and low temperatures of certain cities.

Catchy Headline: The Northeast Is Going South!

- No stacking is used.

|---|---|---|

| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |

- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

raw_comment:
1) What do we notice?
A lot of these cities have temperatures and forecasting that are all over the place. Some of us noticed that the forecast often tends to be inaccurate, compared to real temperatures. There are many cities in which the temperature is exceptionally high for this time of year; we noticed Boston, in particular, because it is somewhat close to us. They have very high temperatures. Some places even experienced rapidly shifting temperatures.

2) We wondered why Ft. Myers has its name. How do people make decisions about forecasting (how do they know how to make a forecast). 

3) How does this relate to us? This winter has also been warm for us, as it has been for many cities...we think this may be due to climate change. We have noticed rapid increases and declines in temperatures in our area; some days we go from 50s to 20s very rapidly.

- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.

- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

|---|---|---|

| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |

A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |
